Let $K$ be a nonempty compact subset of $\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, with its Borel sigma-algebra, and let $a:K\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. The **convex hull** $\operatorname{conv}K$ is the set of finite convex combinations of points of $K$. A **phase generator** is a point $y\in K$ with declared energy $a(y)$. A **mixture** is a Borel probability measure $P$ on $K$. Its barycenter and mean energy are the coordinatewise Lebesgue integrals
$$\bar y(P):=\int_K y\,dP(y)\in\mathbb R^d,\qquad \bar a(P):=\int_K a(y)\,dP(y)\in\mathbb R.$$
These integrals are finite because each coordinate and $a$ are bounded on compact $K$. For prescribed mean $x\in\operatorname{conv}K$, the **mixture energy** is
$$a_{\rm mix}(x):=\inf\{\bar a(P):P\text{ is a Borel probability on }K,\ \bar y(P)=x\}.$$
The admissible set is nonempty since every finite convex combination of points of $K$ is the barycenter of a finite atomic probability. The definition does not assert that the infimum is attained; the theorem on this page gives a compact continuous sufficient condition.

Let $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty compact, $d\ge1$, and $a:K\to\mathbb R$ continuous. Define $a_{\rm mix}$ as in [[def-tdmath-mixture-generator-space-and-energy]]. Then for every $x\in\operatorname{conv}K$ the infimum defining $a_{\rm mix}(x)$ is attained by a Borel probability measure supported on at most $d+1$ points. The function $a_{\rm mix}$ is lower semicontinuous and convex on $\operatorname{conv}K$, and is the greatest convex function on $\operatorname{conv}K$ bounded above by $a$ on $K$. Minimizing over all Borel probabilities on $K$ gives the same attained value as minimizing over finite mixtures. This is a mathematical compactness result; it makes no phase-preparation or equilibrium postulate.

derivations.claim: For each integer $n\ge2$, the set $E_n=[1/n,1)$ is Borel, and $\bigcup_{n\ge2}E_n=(0,1)$. Since $P((0,1))=1$, countable subadditivity implies $P(E_n)>0$ for at least one $n$; otherwise the union would have probability zero. On $E_n$, $x\ge1/n$, while elsewhere $x\ge0$, so $$\int_{(0,1)}x\,dP\ge \frac1nP(E_n)>0.$$ Therefore every admissible probability has strictly positive objective. [A1, F1, algebra]

The point mass $\delta_{1/n}$ at $1/n$ is a Borel probability on $(0,1)$ and has objective $1/n$. These values tend to zero, while 1.1 shows all objectives are positive. Hence the infimum is zero and is not attained. The generator set is noncompact, so this conclusion does not contradict the compact result [F2]; it shows why an attainment theorem must retain its compactness/coercivity hypotheses. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1] ∎

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

derivations.claim: Since $e_{N,k}\ge1$, $e^{Ne_{N,k}^2}\ge e^N$. For $x\ge e^N$, $x-1\le\lfloor x\rfloor\le x$, so $$e_{N,k}^2+\frac1N\log(1-e^{-N})\le \frac1N\log g_{N,k}\le e_{N,k}^2.$$ The error tends to zero uniformly in $k$. The grid mesh is $1/N$; for a continuous function on $[1,2]$, uniform continuity makes its grid maxima converge to its interval maximum. [A1, F1, F2]

Let $Z_N(b)=\sum_{k=0}^Ng_{N,k}e^{-Nb e_{N,k}}$ and $m_N=\max_k[N^{-1}\log g_{N,k}-b e_{N,k}]$. The largest summand is $e^{Nm_N}$ and there are $N+1$ summands, so $$m_N\le N^{-1}\log Z_N(b)\le m_N+N^{-1}\log(N+1).$$ By 1.1, $m_N\to\max_{e\in[1,2]}(e^2-be)$. If $e=\theta\cdot1+(1-\theta)\cdot2$ with $0<\theta<1$, direct expansion gives $$e^2-be=\theta(1-b)+(1-\theta)(4-2b)-\theta(1-\theta),$$ strictly below the weighted endpoint values. Thus the maximum is at an endpoint and equals $\max(1-b,4-2b)$. [A1, A2, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

For compact $K\subset(1,2)$, strict convexity gives $$\eta:=\min_{e\in K}\left[\max(1-b,4-2b)-(e^2-be)\right]>0$$ by [F3]. Uniform approximation in 1.1 makes every grid exponent in $K$ at most the maximum minus $\eta/2$ for all sufficiently large $N$. On the other hand, an endpoint group has exponent tending to the maximum. Therefore the canonical probability of $K$ is at most $(N+1)e^{-N\eta/2+o(N)}$, which tends to zero. [A1, A2, F1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1]

Choose integers $k_N$ with $e_{N,k_N}\to e\in(1,2)$. The microcanonical exact-group law has energy density exactly $e_{N,k_N}$ at every state. By 1.1 its entropy density $N^{-1}\log g_{N,k_N}$ tends to $e^2$. Thus, for example at the crossing $b=3$, canonical mass escapes every compact neighborhood of any interior target while the microcanonical group remains there. Finally $s(3/2)=9/4<5/2=(s(1)+s(2))/2$, so $s(e)=e^2$ is not concave. The example is a constructed model, not an observation about a material. [A1, A2, step 1.1, step 3.1] ∎

A **symplectic form** on a smooth manifold $M$ is a smooth two-form $\omega$
such that

1. $d\omega=0$, and
2. $(T_pM,\omega_p)$ is a [[def-symplectic-vector-space|symplectic vector
   space]] for every $p\in M$.

The pair $(M,\omega)$ is a **symplectic manifold**. Thus both closedness and
pointwise nondegeneracy are required. A zero-dimensional manifold with its
zero two-form satisfies the definition.

For $H\in C^\infty(M)$, its **Hamiltonian vector field** is the vector field
$X_H$ determined by the library sign convention

$$\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH.$$

A vector field $X$ is **Hamiltonian** if $\iota_X\omega=dH$ for some smooth
function $H$; such an $H$ is a **Hamiltonian function for $X$**. A function and
its vector field are distinct data, and completeness of $X_H$ is not assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(M,\omega)$ be a smooth $2n$-dimensional symplectic manifold and $H\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$, with Hamiltonian field defined by $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$. Wherever its local flow $\phi_t$ is defined, it preserves the symplectic form and the volume measure $m$ determined by $\omega^n/n!$. No completeness is asserted. For a region $R$ on which a nonzero-time map $T=\phi_\tau$ and all its iterates are defined, $T$ is a measure-preserving transformation. If $m(R)<\infty$, then for every measurable $E\subseteq R$, almost every point of $E$ returns to $E$ infinitely often under forward iteration.

If $m(R)=1$ and $T$ is ergodic, then for every $f\in L^1(R,m)$ the averages $N^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}f(T^jx)$ converge almost everywhere and in $L^1$ to $\int_Rf\,dm$. Without ergodicity, the limit is the invariant conditional expectation supplied by Birkhoff's theorem, not necessarily the space mean. Finally, if each stated time map $\phi_t$ is a diffeomorphism of a finite invariant region $R$, a density $p_0\ge0$ with $\int_Rp_0\,dm=1$ and $\int_R|p_0\log p_0|\,dm<\infty$ transports by $p_t=p_0\circ\phi_{-t}$ with conserved fine-grained entropy $-k_B\int_Rp_t\log p_t\,dm$, using $0\log0=0$. Volume preservation alone does not imply ergodicity or a time-average/ensemble identity.

A measure-preserving system is **ergodic for $\mu$** if each $E\in\mathcal I$ has $\mu(E)=0$ or $\mu(X\setminus E)=0$, with $\mathcal I$ as in [[def-strict-and-mod-null-invariant-sigma-algebras]]. For a probability system this means $\mu(E)\in\{0,1\}$. The definition is relative to the invariant measure; no probability assumption is implicit in the general null/conull formulation.

derivations.claim: Write $X_H=a\partial_q+b\partial_p$. Then $\iota_{X_H}(dq\wedge dp)=a\,dp-b\,dq$, while $dH=-\sin q\,dq$. Equating coefficients gives $a=0$ and $b=\sin q$. The explicit solution is $$\phi_t(q,p)=(q,p+t\sin q\pmod{2\pi}),$$ which is defined for every real $t$ and is a diffeomorphism with inverse $\phi_{-t}$. [A1, F1, algebra]

Since $H\circ\phi_t=H$, the set $A$ is invariant under every $\phi_t$. The torus has total area $(2\pi)^2=4\pi^2$. The allowed $q$ values in $A$ have total length $\pi$, while $p$ ranges over length $2\pi$, so $m(A)=2\pi^2$, strictly between zero and total area. The map preserves area by [F2], and the invariant set violates the criterion [F3]; hence it is not ergodic for any nonzero sampling time. [A1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the exact first-clause interface of [[thm-tdmath-general-trace-gibbs-model]]: a nonzero complex Hilbert space has a finite or countable complete orthonormal energy eigenbasis $(u_j)$ for a self-adjoint semibounded $A$, with each energy eigenspace finite-dimensional. The supplier is a current draft whose statement and complete argument have been inspected; this theorem is conditional on that interface and does not claim its independent acceptance. Let $\hbar>0$, define $U_tu_j=e^{-iE_jt/\hbar}u_j$, and extend linearly and continuously. For any positive trace-class density operator $\rho$ with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, set $\rho_t=U_t\rho U_t^*$. If $P_E$ denotes the projection onto the full eigenspace of energy $E$, then the trace-norm Riemann average
$$\bar\rho_T:=\frac1T\int_0^T\rho_t\,dt$$
converges as $T\to\infty$ to
$$\rho_{\rm diag}:=\sum_E P_E\rho P_E$$
in trace norm. The full degenerate energy blocks are retained. Thus expectations of every bounded observable converge to their diagonal-ensemble values. This asserts Cesàro convergence, not convergence of $\rho_t$ at individual late times, and is restricted to the stated discrete trace-class spectrum.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with

Let $d\ge1$, and let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty compact set of dimensionless phase-generator coordinates. A generator point $x\in K$ encodes one model-specified homogeneous phase state, with declared entropy per mole $s(x)$ in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$; let $s:K\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. Define $\operatorname{conv}K$ as the set of finite convex combinations of points of $K$, and fix $\bar x\in\operatorname{conv}K$. Use the Borel sigma algebra relative to $K$, and let $\delta_x$ denote unit point mass at $x$. The vector integral $\int_Kx\,dP$ is taken coordinatewise. Assume every Borel probability mixture $P$ on $K$ with $\int_Kx\,dP(x)=\bar x$ is feasible and has entropy per mole $\int_Ks(x)\,dP(x)$. Then the entropy maximum over all such mixtures is attained by a finite atomic mixture with at most $d+1$ phase-generator states.

Here the integral uses the measure convention of [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]]. The entropy map includes its physical entropy units and is part of the model; this theorem does not derive the microscopic meaning of entropy or assert that a physical phase domain is compact.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

A measure space is a triple $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ where $\Sigma$ contains $\varnothing,X$ and is closed under complements and countable unions (a $\sigma$-algebra) of subsets of $X$ and $\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ is countably additive with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$. A measurable function $f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]$ has measurable inverse images of Borel sets, where the Borel sets of the extended real line are the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets. A nonnegative simple function has the form $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ with finitely many disjoint $A_j\in\Sigma$ and finite $c_j\ge0$. Define $c\mu(A)=+\infty$ if $c>0$ and $\mu(A)=+\infty$, define $0\cdot\infty:=0$, and define the finite sum of these extended nonnegative terms to be $+\infty$ if any term is $+\infty$ and otherwise the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Then $\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$; using canonical level sets $\{s=c\}$ makes this value representation-independent. For measurable $f\ge0$, define $\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\{\int s\,d\mu: s\text{ is simple and }0\le s\le f\}$, using [[def-complete-ordered-field]] for a bounded set of finite values and setting the supremum to $+\infty$ when the values are unbounded or one is infinite. A real measurable $f$ is integrable when $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, and then $\int f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$, where $f^+=\max(f,0)$ and $f^-:=\max(-f,0)$. Complex integrability and integration are defined by integrable real and imaginary parts.

Their union is $K$; since $P(K)=1$, countable additivity implies $P(A_n)>0$ for some $n$. On $A_n$, $s\le s_0-a/n$, and on its complement $s\le s_0$. For any nonnegative simple function $\varphi\le s$, the measure integral definition [F2] therefore gives
$$
\int_K\varphi\,dP\le (s_0-a/n)P(A_n)+s_0P(K\setminus A_n)=s_0-aP(A_n)/n<s_0.
$$
Indeed, refine the finitely many level sets of $\varphi$ by $A_n$ and its complement; each simple-function coefficient is bounded by the corresponding pointwise bound on that piece, so the simple-integral formula [F2] gives the inequality. The common strict upper bound is independent of $\varphi$, hence its supremum also satisfies $\int_Ks\,dP<s_0$.

For each $0<\epsilon<1$, the measure $P_\epsilon=\tfrac12\delta_{-\epsilon}+\tfrac12\delta_{\epsilon}$ is supported on $K$, has mean zero, and satisfies $\int s\,dP_\epsilon=s_0-a\epsilon$. Letting $\epsilon\downarrow0$ shows that the supremum is $s_0$. Step 1.1 shows that no feasible measure attains it. $$
\mathcal U_i(\lambda s,\lambda V,\lambda n)=\lambda\mathcal U_i(s,V,n)
$$
for all $\lambda$ in a neighborhood of $1$ for which the scaled state remains in the chart. This is a phase-branch hypothesis: the general tagged law of [[post-td-bulk-additivity]] does not imply it. It may be stipulated independently on each local branch, or supplied by the common-law bulk subclass of [[pthm-td-euler-and-gibbs-duhem]] when each phase's local inverse states lie in its designated entropy cone with fixed species and intensive parameters and common SI units and energy/entropy reference conventions. That supplied subclass uses local inverse uniqueness and does not require a global energy inverse.

Suppose a state $(T_0,p_0)\in O$ is an attained interior coexistence equilibrium with bilateral energy, volume, and species exchange between the two branches, and both branches admit the valid local Gibbs charts of [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]. Write $g_i=G_i/n_i$, $s_i=S_i/n_i$, and $v_i=V_i/n_i$ in the units specified by [[def-td-si-quantities]]. If
$$
\Delta v(T_0,p_0):=v_\beta(T_0,p_0)-v_\alpha(T_0,p_0)\ne0,

$$
\frac{dp}{dT}=\frac{s_\beta-s_\alpha}{v_\beta-v_\alpha}.
$$
If, in addition, conversion from $\alpha$ to $\beta$ is admitted as a reversible process in contact with an ideal thermal reservoir at the same fixed $T$, then its molar latent heat absorbed by the system is $\ell_{\alpha\to\beta}=T(s_\beta-s_\alpha)$. Let $\alpha,\beta$ be two one-component phase branches from [[def-td-phase-and-coexistence-domain]] on a common open chart $O\subset(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ with coordinates $(T,p)$. Assume each branch has a local $C^2$ energy representation $\mathcal U_i(s,V,n)$, $i\in\{\alpha,\beta\}$, and that within each fixed branch tag it satisfies the same-tag homogeneity
\[
\mathcal U_i(\lambda s,\lambda V,\lambda n)=\lambda\mathcal U_i(s,V,n)
\]
for all $\lambda$ in a neighborhood of $1$ for which the scaled state remains in the chart. This is an additional phase-branch hypothesis: [[post-td-bulk-additivity]] permits the scaled material tag to change and does not imply this identity.

Suppose a state $(T_0,p_0)\in O$ is an attained interior coexistence equilibrium with bilateral energy, volume, and species exchange between the two branches, and both branches admit the valid local Gibbs charts of [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]. Write $g_i=G_i/n_i$, $s_i=S_i/n_i$, and $v_i=V_i/n_i$ in the units specified by [[def-td-si-quantities]]. If
\[
\Delta v(T_0,p_0):=v_\beta(T_0,p_0)-v_\alpha(T_0,p_0)\ne0,
\]
then, on some open interval about $T_0$, the equal-Gibbs-per-mole coexistence condition $g_\alpha(T,p(T))=g_\beta(T,p(T))$ defines a unique local $C^1$ curve and
\[
\frac{dp}{dT}=\frac{s_\beta-s_\alpha}{v_\beta-v_\alpha}.
\]
If, in addition, conversion from $\alpha$ to $\beta$ is admitted as a reversible process in contact with an ideal thermal reservoir at the same fixed $T$, then its molar latent heat absorbed by the system is $\ell_{\alpha\to\beta}=T(s_\beta-s_\alpha)$. $(2m+1)^d-(2m-1)^d$ by [F3]. For $m\ge1$, factor the difference of powers:
$$(2m+1)^d-(2m-1)^d=2\sum_{r=0}^{d-1}(2m+1)^{d-1-r}(2m-1)^r\le2d3^{d-1}m^{d-1},$$

A neighbor of $q_i$ in shell $m=1$ has distance at least $1$ and
contributes at most $c$ in absolute value; there are $3^d-1$ such cells. For
$m\ge2$, choose a coordinate $r$ with $|k_r|=m$. If $k_r=m$, every point of

$k_r=-m$, the absolute difference is greater than $\delta(m-1)$. Hence every
point of $D_k$ is at Euclidean distance at least $\delta(m-1)$ from $q_i$.

total contribution by
$$2d3^{d-1}m^{d-1}c\delta^{-p}(m-1)^{-d-\epsilon}.$$

[F4], every fixed particle satisfies
$$\sum_{j\ne i}|\phi_{\mathrm{att}}(q_i-q_j)|\le C_*:=c(3^d-1)+2d3^{d-1}c\delta^{-p}2^p\sum_{m=2}^{\infty}m^{-1-\epsilon}<\infty.$$

The ordered region becomes $0\leq y_1\leq\cdots\leq y_N\leq S$, where $S=L-(N-1)a$. The cube $[0,S]^N$ splits, up to equality sets of zero product measure, into $N!$ coordinate-order regions. Product-measure uniqueness makes these permutation chambers equal in measure, so the ordered region has volume $S^N/N!$. The full labeled allowed volume is $N!$ times this, and canonical division by $N!$ gives $Z(L,N;\beta)=S^N/N!$.

If $L=(N-1)a$, then $S=0$ and the transformed region is a null set; its integral is zero. If $L>(N-1)a$, then $S>0$ and the ordered region has positive product volume. Thus the maximal-density endpoint does not carry a positive canonical partition at exact close packing; the interior-only theorem [F2] makes no contrary assertion.

cex-tdmath-noncompact-mixture-nonattainm.title: Noncompact mixtures can have an unattained energy infimum

references.title: David Tong, Statistical Physics, complete author-hosted lecture text
references.locator: Complete author-hosted HTML chapter read; §§1.2–1.4, finite canonical and microcanonical ensemble conventions.

references.title: Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics

cex-tdmath-noncompact-mixture-nonattainm.statement: For every nonempty Borel generator set $K$ and continuous energy $a:K\to\mathbb R$ bounded below, the unconstrained infimum of $\int_Ka\,dP$ over Borel probability measures on $K$ is attained whenever it is finite, without a compactness or coercivity hypothesis.
cex-tdmath-noncompact-mixture-nonattainm.example: Extend the objective in [[def-tdmath-mixture-generator-space-and-energy]] to the noncompact Borel generator set $K=(0,1)$ with energy $a(x)=x$, and impose no barycenter constraint. The infimum of $\int_Kx\,dP(x)$ over Borel probability measures is $0$, but no probability measure attains it. Thus compactness and the stated feasibility conditions in [[thm-tdmath-compact-continuous-mixture-attainment]] cannot be discarded in a general attainment claim.
cex-tdmath-noncompact-mixture-nonattainm.proof:
**Given:** [A1] and the mixture objective [F1].

1.1 For each integer $n\ge2$, the set $E_n=[1/n,1)$ is Borel, and $\bigcup_{n\ge2}E_n=(0,1)$. Since $P((0,1))=1$, countable subadditivity implies $P(E_n)>0$ for at least one $n$; otherwise the union would have probability zero. On $E_n$, $x\ge1/n$, while elsewhere $x\ge0$, so $$\int_{(0,1)}x\,dP\ge \frac1nP(E_n)>0.$$ Therefore every admissible probability has strictly positive objective. [A1, F1, algebra]

2.1 The point mass $\delta_{1/n}$ at $1/n$ is a Borel probability on $(0,1)$ and has objective $1/n$. These values tend to zero, while 1.1 shows all objectives are positive. Hence the infimum is zero and is not attained. The generator set is noncompact, so this conclusion does not contradict the compact result [F2]; it shows why an attainment theorem must retain its compactness/coercivity hypotheses. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1] ∎

cex-tdmath-nonconcave-ensemble-inequival.title: A controlled nonconcave entropy model with ensemble inequivalence

references.title: David Tong, Statistical Physics, complete author-hosted lecture text
references.locator: Complete author-hosted HTML chapter read; §§1.2–1.4, finite canonical and microcanonical ensemble conventions.

references.title: Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics
references.locator: Complete 635-page lecture notes retrieved and read; §§4.2–4.6, pp.192–217, ensembles, microcanonical phase space, quantum density matrices, and traces.

cex-tdmath-nonconcave-ensemble-inequival.statement: For every sequence of finite systems with admissible exact-group microcanonical energy densities tending to an interior value $e$, there is a fixed positive inverse temperature for which the canonical energy density concentrates at $e$ as system size tends to infinity, without further hypotheses such as entropy concavity.
cex-tdmath-nonconcave-ensemble-inequival.example:
Fix an energy scale $\varepsilon>0$. For each $N\ge1$ and $k=0,\ldots,N$, set $e_{N,k}=1+k/N$, $E_{N,k}=N\varepsilon e_{N,k}$, and
$$g_{N,k}:=\left\lfloor e^{N e_{N,k}^2}\right\rfloor.$$
Construct the finite state set $\{(k,j):0\le k\le N,\ 1\le j\le g_{N,k}\}$ with energy $E_{N,k}$ for each state in group $k$. Its dimensionless exact-group entropy density tends uniformly on the grid to $s(e)=e^2$ on $[1,2]$, which is nonconcave. For fixed inverse temperature $\beta>0$, put $b=\beta\varepsilon$ and let $p_N(b)$ be the canonical log partition sum per site. Then
$$p_N(b)\longrightarrow\max_{1\le e\le2}(e^2-be)=\max(1-b,4-2b).$$
For every compact $K\subset(1,2)$, the canonical probability that the energy density lies in $K$ tends to zero, while an exact microcanonical group with $e_{N,k_N}\to e\in(1,2)$ is supported at that interior density and has entropy density tending to $e^2$. This is an explicit constructed finite sequence demonstrating that ensemble equivalence does not follow from large $N$ alone.
cex-tdmath-nonconcave-ensemble-inequival.proof:
**Given:** [A1]–[A2] and [F1]–[F3].

1.1 Since $e_{N,k}\ge1$, $e^{Ne_{N,k}^2}\ge e^N$. For $x\ge e^N$, $x-1\le\lfloor x\rfloor\le x$, so $$e_{N,k}^2+\frac1N\log(1-e^{-N})\le \frac1N\log g_{N,k}\le e_{N,k}^2.$$ The error tends to zero uniformly in $k$. The grid mesh is $1/N$; for a continuous function on $[1,2]$, uniform continuity makes its grid maxima converge to its interval maximum. [A1, F1, F2]

2.1 Let $Z_N(b)=\sum_{k=0}^Ng_{N,k}e^{-Nb e_{N,k}}$ and $m_N=\max_k[N^{-1}\log g_{N,k}-b e_{N,k}]$. The largest summand is $e^{Nm_N}$ and there are $N+1$ summands, so $$m_N\le N^{-1}\log Z_N(b)\le m_N+N^{-1}\log(N+1).$$ By 1.1, $m_N\to\max_{e\in[1,2]}(e^2-be)$. If $e=\theta\cdot1+(1-\theta)\cdot2$ with $0<\theta<1$, direct expansion gives $$e^2-be=\theta(1-b)+(1-\theta)(4-2b)-\theta(1-\theta),$$ strictly below the weighted endpoint values. Thus the maximum is at an endpoint and equals $\max(1-b,4-2b)$. [A1, A2, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For compact $K\subset(1,2)$, strict convexity gives $$\eta:=\min_{e\in K}\left[\max(1-b,4-2b)-(e^2-be)\right]>0$$ by [F3]. Uniform approximation in 1.1 makes every grid exponent in $K$ at most the maximum minus $\eta/2$ for all sufficiently large $N$. On the other hand, an endpoint group has exponent tending to the maximum. Therefore the canonical probability of $K$ is at most $(N+1)e^{-N\eta/2+o(N)}$, which tends to zero. [A1, A2, F1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 Choose integers $k_N$ with $e_{N,k_N}\to e\in(1,2)$. The microcanonical exact-group law has energy density exactly $e_{N,k_N}$ at every state. By 1.1 its entropy density $N^{-1}\log g_{N,k_N}$ tends to $e^2$. Thus, for example at the crossing $b=3$, canonical mass escapes every compact neighborhood of any interior target while the microcanonical group remains there. Finally $s(3/2)=9/4<5/2=(s(1)+s(2))/2$, so $s(e)=e^2$ is not concave. The example is a constructed model, not an observation about a material. [A1, A2, step 1.1, step 3.1] ∎

cex-tdmath-nonergodic-volume-flow.title: A finite-volume Hamiltonian map that is not ergodic

references.title: David Tong, Kinetic Theory, Part 2
references.locator: Complete 39-page lecture-note part retrieved and read; §2.1, pp.14–16, Liouville phase-space volume; §§2.2–2.3, pp.20–35, Boltzmann equation and H-theorem.

references.locator: Complete author-hosted HTML chapter read; §§8.1–8.3, Hamiltonian phase-space flow, Liouville theorem, and equilibration qualifications.

cex-tdmath-nonergodic-volume-flow.statement: Every nonzero-time map of a complete Hamiltonian flow preserving finite symplectic volume is ergodic with respect to the normalized volume measure.
cex-tdmath-nonergodic-volume-flow.example: On the symplectic torus $\mathbb T^2=(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)^2$ with $\omega=dq\wedge dp$, let $H(q,p)=\cos q$. The Hamiltonian flow is complete and preserves finite area, but every nonzero-time map is nonergodic: the invariant set $A=\{(q,p):\cos q>0\}$ has exactly half the total area. This gives a concrete reason volume preservation alone cannot identify time averages with whole-space ensemble averages.
cex-tdmath-nonergodic-volume-flow.proof:
**Given:** [A1] and the canonical convention [F1].

1.1 Write $X_H=a\partial_q+b\partial_p$. Then $\iota_{X_H}(dq\wedge dp)=a\,dp-b\,dq$, while $dH=-\sin q\,dq$. Equating coefficients gives $a=0$ and $b=\sin q$. The explicit solution is $$\phi_t(q,p)=(q,p+t\sin q\pmod{2\pi}),$$ which is defined for every real $t$ and is a diffeomorphism with inverse $\phi_{-t}$. [A1, F1, algebra]

2.1 Since $H\circ\phi_t=H$, the set $A$ is invariant under every $\phi_t$. The torus has total area $(2\pi)^2=4\pi^2$. The allowed $q$ values in $A$ have total length $\pi$, while $p$ ranges over length $2\pi$, so $m(A)=2\pi^2$, strictly between zero and total area. The map preserves area by [F2], and the invariant set violates the criterion [F3]; hence it is not ergodic for any nonzero sampling time. [A1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

ex-tdmath-pure-state-versus-average-entr.title: Pure-state entropy and entropy of a dephased average

references.title: Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics

ex-tdmath-pure-state-versus-average-entr.statement: Let $u_1,u_2$ be orthonormal energy eigenvectors with distinct energies $E_1\ne E_2$, and let $\psi=(u_1+u_2)/\sqrt2$, $\rho=|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|$. Define the finite-dimensional entropy of a density matrix with eigenvalues $p_i$ as $S(\rho)=-k_B\sum_i p_i\log p_i$, with $0\log0=0$ and fixed $k_B>0$. Every instantaneous unitary state $\rho_t$ is pure and has entropy zero. The Cesàro states converge to $\rho_{\rm diag}=(P_1+P_2)/2$, whose entropy is $k_B\log2$. In fact $S(\bar\rho_T)\to k_B\log2$, whereas $T^{-1}\int_0^T S(\rho_t)\,dt=0$ for every $T$. Entropy of the averaged state and average instantaneous entropy are distinct quantities.
ex-tdmath-pure-state-versus-average-entr.example: Let $u_1,u_2$ be orthonormal energy eigenvectors with distinct energies $E_1\ne E_2$, and let $\psi=(u_1+u_2)/\sqrt2$, $\rho=|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|$. Define the finite-dimensional entropy of a density matrix with eigenvalues $p_i$ as $S(\rho)=-k_B\sum_i p_i\log p_i$, with $0\log0=0$ and fixed $k_B>0$. Every instantaneous unitary state $\rho_t$ is pure and has entropy zero. The Cesàro states converge to $\rho_{\rm diag}=(P_1+P_2)/2$, whose entropy is $k_B\log2$. In fact $S(\bar\rho_T)\to k_B\log2$, whereas $T^{-1}\int_0^T S(\rho_t)\,dt=0$ for every $T$. Entropy of the averaged state and average instantaneous entropy are distinct quantities.
ex-tdmath-pure-state-versus-average-entr.proof:
**Given:** [A1] and the entropy convention.

1.1 The unitary evolution sends $\psi$ to $(e^{-iE_1t/\hbar}u_1+e^{-iE_2t/\hbar}u_2)/\sqrt2$, which remains a unit vector by [F2]. Its rank-one density has eigenvalues $1,0$, so its entropy is $-k_B(1\log1+0\log0)=0$ for every $t$. [A1, F2, algebra]

2.1 The two energy eigenspaces are one-dimensional. The dephasing theorem [F1] removes their off-diagonal matrix entries and yields $\rho_{\rm diag}=\tfrac12P_1+\tfrac12P_2$. Its eigenvalues are $(1/2,1/2)$, so $$S(\rho_{\rm diag})=-k_B\left(\tfrac12\log\tfrac12+\tfrac12\log\tfrac12\right)=k_B\log2.$$ Since every $S(\rho_t)=0$, the time average of instantaneous entropy is exactly zero. [A1, F1, F3, step 1.1]

3.1 In the basis $(u_1,u_2)$, $\bar\rho_T$ has diagonal entries $1/2$ and off-diagonal entry $$c_T=\frac1{2T}\int_0^T e^{-i(E_1-E_2)t/\hbar}\,dt,$$ whose magnitude is at most $\hbar/(T|E_1-E_2|)$ by direct integration. Its eigenvalues are $1/2\pm|c_T|$, so both tend to $1/2$. Continuity of $x\mapsto-x\log x$ at $1/2$ gives $S(\bar\rho_T)\to k_B\log2$. Thus entropy of the averaged state has a nonzero limit even though the averaged instantaneous entropy remains zero. [A1, F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

cex-td-noncompact-phase-mixture-no-attai.title: A noncompact phase domain with no attained mixture maximum
cex-td-noncompact-phase-mixture-no-attai.physical_scope: A constructed continuous concave entropy functional on a noncompact phase-generator domain; it shows that the compactness hypothesis in the mixture-attainment result cannot simply be dropped.

references.title: David Tong, Statistical Physics, author-hosted complete lecture notes, §5.4.3
Konstantin K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics: Statistical Mechanics, §4.1 First-order phase transitions

cex-td-noncompact-phase-mixture-no-attai.statement: Every nonempty feasible family of Borel probability mixtures on a noncompact phase-generator domain, with a prescribed barycenter and bounded positive continuous concave generator entropy, attains its finite entropy supremum without an additional compactness or coercivity hypothesis.
cex-td-noncompact-phase-mixture-no-attai.example:
Let the one-dimensional phase-generator domain be $K=(-1,0)\cup(0,1)$, which is noncompact, and let its dimensionless coordinate be $x$. Assign entropy per mole
$$
s(x)=s_0-a|x|,\qquad a>0,
$$
where $s_0>a>0$ have units $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$. Consider all Borel probability mixtures on $K$ with fixed barycenter $\bar x=0$ and declare them feasible with entropy $\int_Ks\,dP$. This is a constructed mixture model, not a claim that a particular material has this phase domain.
cex-td-noncompact-phase-mixture-no-attai.proof:
1.1 Since $0< s_0-a\le s(x)\le s_0$, every feasible $s$ is nonnegative and bounded. For $n\ge2$, put $A_n:=\{x\in K:|x|\ge1/n\}$. Their union is $K$; since $P(K)=1$, countable additivity implies $P(A_n)>0$ for some $n$. On $A_n$, $s\le s_0-a/n$, and on its complement $s\le s_0$. For any nonnegative simple function $\varphi\le s$, the measure integral definition [F2] therefore gives
$$
\int_K\varphi\,dP\le (s_0-a/n)P(A_n)+s_0P(K\setminus A_n)=s_0-aP(A_n)/n<s_0.
$$
Indeed, refine the finitely many level sets of $\varphi$ by $A_n$ and its complement; each simple-function coefficient is bounded by the corresponding pointwise bound on that piece, so the simple-integral formula [F2] gives the inequality. The common strict upper bound is independent of $\varphi$, hence its supremum also satisfies $\int_Ks\,dP<s_0$. [given, F2, algebra]

2.1 For each $0<\epsilon<1$, the measure $P_\epsilon=\tfrac12\delta_{-\epsilon}+\tfrac12\delta_{\epsilon}$ is supported on $K$, has mean zero, and satisfies $\int s\,dP_\epsilon=s_0-a\epsilon$. Letting $\epsilon\downarrow0$ shows that the supremum is $s_0$. Step 1.1 shows that no feasible measure attains it. This lies outside the compactness hypothesis in [F1] and exhibits a finite supremum without a maximizing mixture. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

cex-td-clapeyron-zero-volume-jump.title: Equal branch volumes do not give a Clapeyron graph
cex-td-clapeyron-zero-volume-jump.physical_scope: A constructed pair of smooth one-component Gibbs charts with zero molar-volume jump; it shows why the local nonzero-jump hypothesis cannot be omitted and makes no material claim.

references.title: David Tong, Statistical Physics, author-hosted complete lecture notes, §§5.1.1–5.1.2
Konstantin K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics: Statistical Mechanics, §4.1 First-order phase transitions

cex-td-clapeyron-zero-volume-jump.statement: Equality of two smooth one-component molar Gibbs branches near a coexistence point always defines a unique differentiable pressure graph $p=p(T)$ on an open temperature interval, with slope $\Delta s/\Delta v$, even when the molar-volume jump $\Delta v$ vanishes.
cex-td-clapeyron-zero-volume-jump.example:
Fix $T_0>0$, $p_0>0$, $g_0\in\mathbb R$, $v_0,c,\kappa>0$, and distinct positive molar entropies $s_\alpha,s_\beta$. Use units $g_0\in\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$, $v_0\in\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$, $c\in\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, and $\kappa\in\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}Pa^{-1}}$. On a common open chart define
$$
g_i(T,p)=g_0-s_i(T-T_0)-\frac{c}{2T_0}(T-T_0)^2+v_0(p-p_0)-\frac{\kappa}{2}(p-p_0)^2,
$$
with $i\in\{\alpha,\beta\}$. Let $G_i=n_i g_i$ and adopt $S_i=-\partial_TG_i$, $V_i=\partial_pG_i$, $\mu_i=\partial_{n_i}G_i$, and $U_i=G_i+TS_i-pV_i$. This gives same-tag scaling and smooth local Gibbs charts. At $(T_0,p_0)$ the molar Gibbs values agree and the molar-volume jump is zero; the entropies differ.
cex-td-clapeyron-zero-volume-jump.proof:
1.1 At $(T_0,p_0)$, differentiation gives $S_i/n_i=s_i$, $V_i/n_i=v_0$, and $\mu_i=g_i=g_0$. Also $U_{i,T}=n_i c$, $V_{i,p}=-n_i\kappa$, and $V_{i,T}=0$, so the derivative determinant for $(T,p)\mapsto(U_i,V_i)$ at fixed positive amount is $-n_i^2c\kappa\ne0$. Thus [L1] supplies valid local state charts. The branch equality function is
$$
F(T,p):=g_\beta-g_\alpha=-(s_\beta-s_\alpha)(T-T_0),
$$
whose zero set is $T=T_0$ with every nearby chart pressure permitted. [given, A1, L1, algebra]

2.1 Here $\Delta v=v_\beta-v_\alpha=0$, so the zero set is not the graph of a unique pressure as a function of temperature on an open interval about $T_0$, and the quotient $\Delta s/\Delta v$ is undefined. The nonzero-jump hypothesis of [F1] fails, so this model does not contradict that theorem. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

cex-tdmath-bulk-field-pressure.title: A volume-sized external field changes ideal-gas pressure

references.title: D. Dereudre, Introduction to the theory of Gibbs point processes
references.locator: Section 1.3, PDF pp.10–12: finite-volume grand-canonical normalization; the calculation is derived directly here.

cex-tdmath-bulk-field-pressure.statement: At fixed activity $z>0$ and inverse temperature $\beta>0$, adding any spatially constant one-particle external energy throughout a continuum ideal-gas region leaves the thermodynamic-limit log grand partition sum per volume unchanged, as would a negligible boundary perturbation.
cex-tdmath-bulk-field-pressure.proof:
**Given:** $V>0$, $z>0$, $\beta>0$, constant $c\in\mathbb R$, and the $1/N!$-normalized positional grand sum.

For the continuum ideal gas in a bounded measurable region $\Omega$ of volume $V$, use activity $z>0$, inverse temperature $\beta>0$, and no pair interaction. Add a constant external one-particle energy $c$ throughout $\Omega$. This volume-sized field changes the pressure per volume whenever $c\ne0$, so it is not a negligible boundary perturbation.

1.1 The $N$-particle term without the field is $z^NV^N/N!$, by the product volume [F1] and the $1/N!$ convention [given]. Summing over $N\geq0$ gives $\Xi_0=\sum_N(zV)^N/N!=e^{zV}$ by [F2]. [given, A1, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 With the field, each term is multiplied by $e^{-\beta cN}$, so $\Xi_c=\sum_N(ze^{-\beta c}V)^N/N!=e^{ze^{-\beta c}V}$ by [F2]. Therefore $V^{-1}\log\Xi_0=z$ and $V^{-1}\log\Xi_c=ze^{-\beta c}$. If $c\ne0$, these differ because $z,\beta>0$. [given, A1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

ex-tdmath-repulsive-power-tail.statement:
Fix $d\ge1$ and $\epsilon>0$. Define
$$\phi_{\mathrm{rep}}(x):=\begin{cases}+\infty,&x=0,\\\|x\|_2^{-d-\epsilon},&x\ne0.\end{cases}$$
This is an even, Borel-measurable stable power-tempered pair potential. It has
an unbounded repulsive core and a nonzero algebraic tail.
ex-tdmath-repulsive-power-tail.example:
Fix $d\ge1$ and $\epsilon>0$. Define
$$\phi_{\mathrm{rep}}(x):=\begin{cases}+\infty,&x=0,\\\|x\|_2^{-d-\epsilon},&x\ne0.\end{cases}$$
This is an even, Borel-measurable stable power-tempered pair potential. It has
an unbounded repulsive core and a nonzero algebraic tail.
ex-tdmath-repulsive-power-tail.proof:
1.1 The norm is continuous, so on $\mathbb R^d\setminus\{0\}$ the function
$x\mapsto\|x\|_2^{-d-\epsilon}$ is continuous by [F2]. The complement of
$\{0\}$ is Borel and $\{0\}$ is closed, so the piecewise function is Borel;
it is even because $\|-x\|_2=\|x\|_2$. For $\|x\|_2\ge1$ it satisfies the
tail bound with $C=1$ and $R=1$. [given, F1, F2]

2.1 Every pair term is nonnegative or $+\infty$. Thus every finite pair sum
satisfies $U_N\ge0$, so the stability constant is $B=0$. This proves the
claimed model-class membership. [F1, given, algebra] ∎

ex-tdmath-hard-core-attractive-power-tai.statement:
Fix an integer $d\ge1$ and constants $c,\epsilon>0$. Set $p=d+\epsilon$ and
define the even radial pair potential
$$\phi_{\mathrm{att}}(x):=\begin{cases}+\infty,&\|x\|_2<1,\\-c\|x\|_2^{-p},&\|x\|_2\ge1.\end{cases}$$
It has a hard core and a nonzero attractive power tail.
ex-tdmath-hard-core-attractive-power-tai.example:
Fix an integer $d\ge1$ and constants $c,\epsilon>0$. Set $p=d+\epsilon$ and
define the even radial pair potential
$$\phi_{\mathrm{att}}(x):=\begin{cases}+\infty,&\|x\|_2<1,\\-c\|x\|_2^{-p},&\|x\|_2\ge1.\end{cases}$$
It has a hard core and a nonzero attractive power tail.
ex-tdmath-hard-core-attractive-power-tai.proof:
1.1 The norm is continuous and $r\mapsto r^{-p}$ is continuous on $r>0$ by
[F2]. The regions $\{\|x\|_2<1\}$ and $\{\|x\|_2\ge1\}$ are Borel, so the
piecewise potential is Borel; radiality makes it even. For $\|x\|_2\ge1$,
$|\phi_{\mathrm{att}}(x)|=c\|x\|_2^{-d-\epsilon}$, so it is power-tempered
with $C=c$ and $R=1$. [given, F1, F2]

1.2 Put $\delta:=1/(2\sqrt d)$. For a fixed particle $q_i$, the half-open
cubes $D_k:=q_i+\delta k+[0,\delta)^d$, $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, partition
$\mathbb R^d$. Their Euclidean diameters are at most $\sqrt d\,\delta=1/2<1$.
The example's definition makes every pair at distance less than $1$ forbidden,
so centers in a finite-energy configuration are separated by at least $1$.
Thus each cube contains at most one center and $D_0$ contains no center other
than $q_i$. The cells in max-norm shell $m$ number
$(2m+1)^d-(2m-1)^d$ by [F3]. For $m\ge1$, factor the difference of powers:
$$(2m+1)^d-(2m-1)^d=2\sum_{r=0}^{d-1}(2m+1)^{d-1-r}(2m-1)^r\le2d3^{d-1}m^{d-1},$$
since $2m+1\le3m$. [given, F1, F3, construct, algebra]

2.1 A neighbor of $q_i$ in shell $m=1$ has distance at least $1$ and
contributes at most $c$ in absolute value; there are $3^d-1$ such cells. For
$m\ge2$, choose a coordinate $r$ with $|k_r|=m$. If $k_r=m$, every point of
$D_k$ differs from $q_i$ in coordinate $r$ by at least $\delta m$; if
$k_r=-m$, the absolute difference is greater than $\delta(m-1)$. Hence every
point of $D_k$ is at Euclidean distance at least $\delta(m-1)$ from $q_i$.
By [F2], each such neighbor contributes at most
$c\delta^{-p}(m-1)^{-p}$. The shell count in step 1.2 therefore bounds its
total contribution by
$$2d3^{d-1}m^{d-1}c\delta^{-p}(m-1)^{-d-\epsilon}.$$
[given, F2, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 For $m\ge2$, $m-1\ge m/2$, so the last bound is at most
$2d3^{d-1}c\delta^{-p}2^p m^{-1-\epsilon}$. Summing over shells and using
[F4], every fixed particle satisfies
$$\sum_{j\ne i}|\phi_{\mathrm{att}}(q_i-q_j)|\le C_*:=c(3^d-1)+2d3^{d-1}c\delta^{-p}2^p\sum_{m=2}^{\infty}m^{-1-\epsilon}<\infty.$$
[F3, F4, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For a finite-energy configuration, every pair term is negative and
$$-U_N=\sum_{i<j}|\phi_{\mathrm{att}}(q_i-q_j)|=\frac12\sum_i\sum_{j\ne i}|\phi_{\mathrm{att}}(q_i-q_j)|\le\frac{C_*}{2}N$$
by step 3.1. A configuration containing a forbidden pair has $U_N=+\infty$
and also satisfies the lower bound. Hence the potential is stable with
$B=C_*/2$. Together with step 1.1, this proves membership in the stated
stable power-tempered class. [F1, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

ex-tdmath-hard-core-zero-beta.title: A hard core remains at zero inverse temperature

references.title: H.-O. Georgii, Large deviations and the equivalence of ensembles for Gibbsian particle systems with superstable interaction
references.locator: Theorem 4, printed p.177 / PDF p.7: beta=0 source convention; the finite example below spells out hard admissibility.

ex-tdmath-hard-core-zero-beta.statement:
In one spatial dimension, let $\phi(x)=+\infty$ for $|x|<a$ and $0$ otherwise, with $a>0$. On an interval $[0,L]$, define the beta-zero weight by retaining the forbidden-pair exclusion as in [[thm-tdmath-retained-hard-zero-beta-limit]]. If $L>a$, the two-particle canonical partition is
$$Z(L,2;0)=\frac{(L-a)^2}{2},$$
while the unrestricted ideal-gas value is $L^2/2$. Thus the retained hard-core beta-zero ensemble is not the Poisson ideal gas.
ex-tdmath-hard-core-zero-beta.example:
In one spatial dimension, let $\phi(x)=+\infty$ for $|x|<a$ and $0$ otherwise, with $a>0$. On an interval $[0,L]$, define the beta-zero weight by retaining the forbidden-pair exclusion as in [[thm-tdmath-retained-hard-zero-beta-limit]]. If $L>a$, the two-particle canonical partition is
$$Z(L,2;0)=\frac{(L-a)^2}{2},$$
while the unrestricted ideal-gas value is $L^2/2$. Thus the retained hard-core beta-zero ensemble is not the Poisson ideal gas.
ex-tdmath-hard-core-zero-beta.proof:
**Given:** The one-dimensional hard-rod potential and the stated interval.

1.1 On the ordered region $x_1<x_2$, allowed pairs satisfy $x_2\geq x_1+a$, so their volume is $\int_0^{L-a}(L-x_1-a)\,dx_1=(L-a)^2/2$. The coordinate-swap map preserves product Lebesgue measure, so the region $x_2<x_1$ has the same volume; the diagonal has zero product measure. Thus the full labeled allowed volume is $(L-a)^2$, and division by $2!$ gives $Z(L,2;0)=(L-a)^2/2$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 Since $0<a<L$, $(L-a)^2/2<L^2/2$, the unrestricted ideal-gas two-particle canonical term. The strict deficit is caused by the forbidden separation band and remains at beta zero by [F2]. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

ex-tdmath-close-packing-endpoint.title: The close-packing endpoint can have zero canonical weight

references.title: D. Dereudre, Introduction to the theory of Gibbs point processes
references.locator: Section 1.3, PDF pp.10–12: canonical positional normalization; the one-dimensional hard-rod integral is calculated here.

ex-tdmath-close-packing-endpoint.statement:
In one dimension, let the pair potential be infinite when the separation is less than $a>0$, and zero otherwise. For $N\geq1$ labeled rods in $[0,L]$, with canonical positional normalization $1/N!$, write $S=L-(N-1)a$. If $S>0$, translating the ordered coordinates by $y_i=x_i-(i-1)a$ gives
$$Z(L,N;\beta)=\frac{S^N}{N!}=\frac{(L-(N-1)a)^N}{N!},\qquad \beta>0.$$
If $S=0$, the allowed configuration set has zero Lebesgue measure and $Z(L,N;\beta)=0$. Along $N\to\infty$ with $L=(N-1)a$, the density $N/L\to1/a$ while every finite-volume partition is zero. Thus the thermodynamic close-packing endpoint is approached by a sequence of zero-weight finite systems; it is not realized by a positive canonical partition. The interior canonical limit theorem makes no assertion at that endpoint.
ex-tdmath-close-packing-endpoint.example:
In one dimension, let the pair potential be infinite when the separation is less than $a>0$, and zero otherwise. For $N\geq1$ labeled rods in $[0,L]$, with canonical positional normalization $1/N!$, write $S=L-(N-1)a$. If $S>0$, translating the ordered coordinates by $y_i=x_i-(i-1)a$ gives
$$Z(L,N;\beta)=\frac{S^N}{N!}=\frac{(L-(N-1)a)^N}{N!},\qquad \beta>0.$$
If $S=0$, the allowed configuration set has zero Lebesgue measure and $Z(L,N;\beta)=0$. Along $N\to\infty$ with $L=(N-1)a$, the density $N/L\to1/a$ while every finite-volume partition is zero. Thus the thermodynamic close-packing endpoint is approached by a sequence of zero-weight finite systems; it is not realized by a positive canonical partition. The interior canonical limit theorem makes no assertion at that endpoint.
ex-tdmath-close-packing-endpoint.proof:
**Given:** $N\geq1$ and $L\geq(N-1)a$.

1.1 Order the coordinates $0\leq x_1<\cdots<x_N\leq L$. The exclusion constraints are $x_{i+1}-x_i\geq a$. Apply the coordinatewise translation $x_i\mapsto y_i=x_i-(i-1)a$; each one-coordinate translation preserves Lebesgue measure [F5], so product measure is preserved. The ordered region becomes $0\leq y_1\leq\cdots\leq y_N\leq S$, where $S=L-(N-1)a$. The cube $[0,S]^N$ splits, up to equality sets of zero product measure, into $N!$ coordinate-order regions. Product-measure uniqueness makes these permutation chambers equal in measure, so the ordered region has volume $S^N/N!$. The full labeled allowed volume is $N!$ times this, and canonical division by $N!$ gives $Z(L,N;\beta)=S^N/N!$. [F1, F3, F4, F5, algebra]

2.1 If $L=(N-1)a$, then $S=0$ and the transformed region is a null set; its integral is zero. If $L>(N-1)a$, then $S>0$ and the ordered region has positive product volume. Thus the maximal-density endpoint does not carry a positive canonical partition at exact close packing; the interior-only theorem [F2] makes no contrary assertion. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

ex-tdmath-nonunique-variational-minimize.title: Nonunique minimizers allow distinct local accumulation limits

references.title: H.-O. Georgii, Large deviations and the equivalence of ensembles for Gibbsian particle systems with superstable interaction
references.locator: Theorems 1–2, printed pp.178–181 / PDF pp.8–11: stationary variational minimizer set; this example is an abstract consequence, not an asserted phase-transition model.

ex-tdmath-nonunique-variational-minimize.statement: Suppose $J(P)=I(P)+\beta\Phi(P)-\rho(P)\log z$ has two distinct stationary minimizers $P_0\ne P_1$ with equal finite value $m$. Every finite mixture $P_\theta=\theta P_0+(1-\theta)P_1$, $0\leq\theta\leq1$, also minimizes $J$. The sequence of stationary laws alternating between $P_0$ and $P_1$ has two distinct local accumulation points and does not converge. This conditional mathematical example shows why compactness alone yields minimizer-set accumulation; it does not assert a finite-volume ensemble realizes the sequence or that a particular continuum potential exhibits coexistence.
ex-tdmath-nonunique-variational-minimize.example: Suppose $J(P)=I(P)+\beta\Phi(P)-\rho(P)\log z$ has two distinct stationary minimizers $P_0\ne P_1$ with equal finite value $m$. Every finite mixture $P_\theta=\theta P_0+(1-\theta)P_1$, $0\leq\theta\leq1$, also minimizes $J$. The sequence of stationary laws alternating between $P_0$ and $P_1$ has two distinct local accumulation points and does not converge. This conditional mathematical example shows why compactness alone yields minimizer-set accumulation; it does not assert a finite-volume ensemble realizes the sequence or that a particular continuum potential exhibits coexistence.
ex-tdmath-nonunique-variational-minimize.proof:
**Given:** The assumptions above.

1.1 Let $P,R$ be stationary laws of finite specific entropy and let $P_\theta=\theta P+(1-\theta)R$. For a bounded cube $G$, the binary-label chain rule [F3] gives $$ \theta D(P_G\Vert Q_G)+(1-\theta)D(R_G\Vert Q_G) =D((P_\theta)_G\Vert Q_G)+I(S;X_G), $$ where $S$ is the mixture label and $X_G$ the observed configuration. Since $0\leq I(S;X_G)\leq H(S)<\infty$, divide by $|G|$ and take the cube limit [F2]; $H(S)/|G|\to0$, so $I(P_\theta)=\theta I(P)+(1-\theta)I(R)$. The expectation defining $\rho$ is affine. For finite energy densities, $E_{P_\theta}H_G=\theta E_PH_G+(1-\theta)E_RH_G$ for every $G$; dividing by volume and taking limits gives affinity of $\Phi$. Thus $J$ is affine on finite mixtures of finite-$J$ laws. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Applying step 1.1 to $P_0,P_1$ gives $J(P_\theta)=\theta J(P_0)+(1-\theta)J(P_1)=m$, so every mixture is a minimizer. Put $P_{2n}=P_0$ and $P_{2n+1}=P_1$. The even and odd subsequences converge locally to $P_0$ and $P_1$. Since distinct laws differ on a bounded-region measurable event, its indicator is a bounded local test by [F4] with different expectations; the full sequence therefore has no $\tau_L$ limit. Both accumulation points are minimizers. [given, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

changes.new_refuted_statement: For every nonempty Borel generator set $K$ and continuous energy $a:K\to\mathbb R$ bounded below, the unconstrained infimum of $\int_Ka\,dP$ over Borel probability measures on $K$ is attained whenever it is finite, without a compactness or coercivity hypothesis.

For every sequence of finite systems with admissible exact-group microcanonical energy densities tending to an interior value $e$, there is a fixed positive inverse temperature for which the canonical energy density concentrates at $e$ as system size tends to infinity, without further hypotheses such as entropy concavity.
Every nonzero-time map of a complete Hamiltonian flow preserving finite symplectic volume is ergodic with respect to the normalized volume measure.

Every nonempty feasible family of Borel probability mixtures on a noncompact phase-generator domain, with a prescribed barycenter and bounded positive continuous concave generator entropy, attains its finite entropy supremum without an additional compactness or coercivity hypothesis.

Equality of two smooth one-component molar Gibbs branches near a coexistence point always defines a unique differentiable pressure graph $p=p(T)$ on an open temperature interval, with slope $\Delta s/\Delta v$, even when the molar-volume jump $\Delta v$ vanishes.

At fixed activity $z>0$ and inverse temperature $\beta>0$, adding any spatially constant one-particle external energy throughout a continuum ideal-gas region leaves the thermodynamic-limit log grand partition sum per volume unchanged, as would a negligible boundary perturbation.
